excerpt: How a surgery recommendation changes a personal injury claim: what it does to case value, and why insurers scrutinize the decision so closely.

faqs.question: Does needing surgery increase my settlement?
faqs.answer: More severe injuries requiring more extensive treatment may result in higher compensation, but there is no fixed uplift. What matters is the documented treatment, the prognosis and the effect on your life, not the procedure alone.

faqs.question: Should I have surgery my doctor recommends while a claim is pending?
faqs.answer: Follow your physician's medical advice. Declining recommended treatment can harm your recovery, and it also gives the insurer grounds to argue that you failed to mitigate your own losses.

faqs.question: When will I receive my settlement?
faqs.answer: Generally not before your treatment has reached a stable point — what doctors call maximum medical improvement — because that is when the full extent of the injury is known. Settling earlier risks accepting a figure that does not cover care you still need. No rule sets a settlement date. The only hard deadlines are for filing suit: two years from the injury in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). In Georgia motor-vehicle cases an attorney's pre-suit demand must also give the insurer at least 30 days to accept and 40 days to pay (O.C.G.A. § 9-11-67.1).

faqs.question: What if the insurance company makes no offer at all?
faqs.answer: That is not the end of the process. A claim can proceed to formal negotiation or litigation, and an attorney's involvement often changes an insurer's posture where an unrepresented claimant was being ignored.

faqs.question: What should I do if surgery has been recommended after my accident?
faqs.answer: Discuss the details of your case with an experienced attorney before making decisions about settlement. Documenting the recommendation and the reasoning behind it is what allows the claim to account for it.
